title: Lifecycle: stop, pause and sleep
standfirst: Providers use seven words for four behaviours. The only question that matters is what is still running when the machine comes back.
idea: Every provider offers a way to make a machine cheaper while you are not using it. They fall into four behaviours. Disk only: the machine is destroyed and its disk is kept, so files survive and processes do not. Disk and memory: RAM is saved, so the agent's process tree can resume mid-task. Warm memory: the machine is frozen in the host's RAM, which resumes fastest and usually keeps billing for memory. Delete: the disk goes too.

The vocabulary is not standardised. InstaBox calls a memory-preserving freeze “pause” and a power-off “stop”. Agent 37 has both, as sleep and stop. boxd has three parked states plus destroy. Lizard's stop deletes the disk. Boat's API calls a stopped sandbox archived, and its homepage still says “pause billing” even though the docs state there is no pause.

Memory-preserving resume is usually best-effort. Sandboxer restores memory only if a matching machine is free within two minutes; InstaBox reports processesPreserved false when it cold-boots instead; Agent 37 says memory usually survives a wake but not always. Anything that must outlive a pause belongs in a file.

splits.heading: Paused, frozen in place
body: boxd keeps the machine's memory in the host's RAM and resumes it in under a millisecond. Nothing is written to disk, which is why it can come back instantly, and why the memory keeps billing while the machine sits paused.

quote.text: They freeze the VMM process and keep memory, running processes, and open sockets intact.

splits.heading: Paused, written to disk
body: Sandboxer writes memory and device state to disk when a sandbox stops, then reads it back on resume. The read-back depends on a host of the same CPU type being free within two minutes; if none is, the sandbox boots cold with its files intact.

quote.text: Memory is restored on a machine with the same CPU type as the one the sandbox stopped on.

splits.heading: Paused, fast pause keeps files only
body: Lizard's ordinary pause keeps the whole disk, the memory and the running processes. Its fast pause is the files-only variant: it keeps only the files and boots fresh when you resume. Both are called pause, and the difference is whether a half-finished task survives.

quote.text: keeps only the files: the whole disk and `/workspace`. It takes about a second at any memory size … `resume()` boots the sandbox fresh with its files, like a restart

splits.heading: No pause at all
body: Boat has no paused state. A stop removes the virtual machine and keeps a copy of the disk; every resume is a new machine with that disk. The disk itself is kept for fourteen days, after which a resume fails and the work is gone.

quote.text: There is no pause. A stop removes the virtual machine and keeps a copy of the disk.

watchFor: Whether the provider's “pause” keeps RAM, keeps only files, or destroys the machine.
Whether a memory restore is guaranteed or a fallback that silently cold-boots.
What resets: IP address, open sockets, cron timers, systemd units, Docker containers.
Whether stopping a paused machine is allowed; at InstaBox it is an error.
Whether the disk survives a stop at all; at Lizard and Morph, stop deletes it.

rows.note: Sleep keeps memory and processes as a checkpoint and bills disk only; stop keeps the disk and loses memory. A wake that has to rebuild boots fresh, and stopping a sleeper discards its checkpoint.

source.quote: Sleep and stop both release CPU and memory and bill disk alone. A sleeping instance keeps its memory and wakes on the next request; a stopped one loses its memory and stays down until `start`.

rows.note: Standby preserves process and filesystem state and stops memory charges, but external network connections do not survive. Archive exports filesystem changes only and restarts processes with new IDs.

source.quote: The snapshot preserves process and filesystem state, but not external network connections

rows.note: There is no pause. Stop saves the disk, removes the machine and loses memory and hand-started processes; resume boots a new machine from the disk with a new IP.

source.quote: There is no pause. A stop removes the virtual machine and keeps a copy of the disk.

rows.note: Four distinct states: standby keeps RAM frozen and bills it, hibernate writes memory to disk with an ~85 ms wake, stop keeps the disk only, destroy removes everything.

source.quote: They freeze the VMM process and keep memory, running processes, and open sockets intact.

rows.note: Pause saves the filesystem and RAM, so processes resume; a filesystem-only pause is opt-in. Kill is terminal, and the default timeout kills the sandbox after five minutes.

source.quote: When you pause a sandbox, both the sandbox's filesystem and memory state will be saved.

rows.note: Pause keeps memory and running programs and resumes in about a second; stop loses them, and a paused machine cannot be stopped at all. A resume can cold-boot and report processesPreserved false.

source.quote: Pauses a running machine, keeping its memory and running programs.

rows.note: Pause keeps the whole disk, memory and processes; a fast pause keeps files only and resumes like a restart; stop or expiry deletes the sandbox disk, leaving only /workspace and snapshots.

source.quote: A stop (kill or expiration) deletes the sandbox's disk: only files on an attached Persistent Volume at `/workspace` and the snapshots you took remain.

rows.note: Pause snapshots memory and disk and suspends the VM; stop releases the instance and deletes it. Booting a snapshot is a cold boot, while starting one restores memory.

source.quote: Use when you need to preserve the running state of applications, the memory contents, and all processes.

rows.note: Pause freezes the VM with memory and programs intact; stop keeps files and drops memory. Both keep billing storage, and only delete ends the charge.

source.quote: `wake`: it carries on where it was

rows.note: A stop writes memory and device state to disk, so a resume can restore running processes — but only on a machine of the same CPU type within two minutes, otherwise it cold-boots.

source.quote: Memory is restored on a machine with the same CPU type as the one the sandbox stopped on.

rows.note: A warm pause freezes memory and processes and resumes in 100–500 ms; a longer idle period stops the VM, drops memory and starts processes fresh. Open TCP connections do not survive either.

source.quote: The VM is suspended with everything in memory frozen in place. Compute billing stops. The next request resumes it in 100–500ms

rows.note: Stopping ends the session. Persistent sandboxes save their filesystem and restore it into a new session, not RAM; restart background services with the onResume hook.

source.quote: Persistent sandboxes automatically save their filesystem state when stopped and restore it when resumed.
